1240.title: Faith rises and falls
1240.hook: many scholars teach that iman increases with good deeds and decreases with sins
1240.howItsDone: In Muslim teaching, faith is spoken of as rising and falling, with good deeds, prayer and Qur'an recitation as ways to strengthen it; Hanafi and Maturidi scholars hold that the core of belief stays constant while its strength and fruits vary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qadar, the decree, the sixth article. Your line: all by his decree.

Phone batteries have a little icon in the corner. Full, then less, then a red sliver, then you plug it in and watch it climb. The six articles of faith could sound like a list you either have or don't, like a membership card. But the Qur'an and the hadith talk about iman more like that battery. It can be more. It can be less. It can be topped up. Today closes the week, not with a seventh thing to believe, but with a way of holding the six.
screen: `A BATTERY ICON.` → `MORE, LESS, TOPPED UP.` → `A WAY OF HOLDING THE SIX.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred fifteen, a companion worried that his iman was low and heard: an hour, and an hour. Today, the teaching behind that. First, the verse. The Qur'an speaks of Allah sending peace into the hearts of believers, in Pickthall's words, "that they might add faith unto their faith." Faith, in that verse, can grow. Another verse says that when Allah's revelations are recited to believers, their faith increases. Second, the branches. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says iman has many branches. The highest is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. The lowest is moving something harmful out of the road. And modesty, the hadith adds, is a branch too. On this picture, faith reaches all the way down to a rock in the street. Third, the scholars. Al-Bukhari titled a chapter on how faith increases and decreases, and a line of Sunni scholars teaches exactly that: good deeds raise it, sins lower it. Hanafi and Maturidi scholars put it another way: the core of iman, the belief itself, doesn't grow or shrink, but its light and its fruits in a person's life do. Both views are held within Sunni Islam. Last, why it matters. If faith can fall, a low day isn't the end of anything. And if it can rise, the way back up is small and concrete: one branch, one deed, one rock moved out of the road.
screen: `ADD FAITH UNTO THEIR FAITH.` · `FROM THE TESTIMONY TO THE ROAD.` · `TWO WAYS SCHOLARS DESCRIBE IT.` · then, large: `ONE ROCK OUT OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Think of the lowest branch in the hadith, moving something harmful out of the way, and find where that is for you: a box blocking a hallway, a sharp comment you could leave out, a task left in someone's path. Choose one, small and real, and picture yourself doing it start to finish. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted; if not, simply decide.
Faith rises and falls. The teaching that iman can be added to by good deeds and lessened by sins; in the Qur'an's words, faith added to faith. Today's word.
Your line: faith grows. The six are done; tomorrow the theologians begin. See you then.

1241.title: Speaking about Allah
1241.hook: theology reasons about faith with arguments
1241.howItsDone: Islamic theology, 'ilm al-kalam, is taught in seminaries and universities alongside law and hadith, through classic creeds and their commentaries; some scholars, notably Hanbalis, have kept a cautious distance from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith rises and falls, and your line: faith grows. One branch, one deed, one rock out of the road.

A king is arguing with Ibrahim about his Lord. Ibrahim says, my Lord is the one who gives life and causes death. The king says, I give life and cause death too. So Ibrahim changes tack. Allah brings the sun up from the east, he says, so bring it up from the west. And the king, the Qur'an says, was left speechless. That scene is in the second surah. It's not a sermon. It's an argument, made with reasons, against someone who disagrees.
screen: `IBRAHIM AND THE KING.` → `THE SUN FROM THE WEST.` → `AN ARGUMENT, NOT A SERMON.`

segments.voice: Today the path opens a new part, on the people who turned that way of talking about Allah into a whole discipline. First, the word. Kalam means speech, words. The discipline is called 'ilm al-kalam, the science of speech, and its scholars are the mutakallimun, the ones who speak. Writers give more than one reason for the name, but what it does is clear: kalam reasons about the articles of faith with arguments. Second, the license. The Qur'an itself argues. Ibrahim argues with the king. Again and again it points to the heavens and the earth, to night and day, as signs for people who use their minds. And it asks, in Pickthall's words, "Will they not then ponder on the Qur'an?" The mutakallimun took that as permission, even instruction, to think hard. Third, the questions. The six articles raised things the list alone doesn't answer. If Allah is one, how do His many names relate to Him? If everything is by decree, how is a person responsible? Is the Qur'an, Allah's speech, eternal or created? Over the next days this path meets the schools that answered differently: the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'aris, the Maturidis, and their critics. Fourth, the critics. Some scholars, notably in the Hanbali school, warned that arguing about Allah beyond what the texts say could pull people away from them. That caution is part of the story too. So kalam isn't faith replaced by reasoning. It's faith asking questions out loud.
screen: `KALAM: SPEECH, WORDS.` · `THE QUR'AN ITSELF ARGUES.` · `ONE GOD, MANY NAMES?` · then, large: `FAITH ASKING OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Let a question come up that you've carried a while and never quite said: about God, about why things happen, about what a word in a prayer really means. Don't reach for the answer; say the question to yourself clearly, in one sentence, then again, a little more exactly. If you pray, you can bring it with you into prayer; if not, let it sit beside you, asked.
Kalam. Speech; the name for Islamic theology, which reasons about the articles of faith with arguments. Its scholars are the mutakallimun. Today's word.
Your line: faith seeks understanding. Tomorrow, the first of the schools: the Mu'tazilah. Peace be with you.

1242.title: The Mu'tazilah
1242.hook: the theologians who stepped aside, and kept thinking about justice
1242.tomorrow: The trial of the created Qur'an
1242.howItsDone: Students of Islamic theology study the Mu'tazilah as an early school of kalam that stressed Allah's justice and oneness, held that humans truly choose their acts, and taught that the Qur'an was created.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalam, speaking about Allah with arguments, and a faith that seeks understanding.

A mosque in Basra, in Iraq. The teacher al-Hasan al-Basri sits with his students, and someone asks a hard question. A Muslim commits a grave sin. Is he still a believer, or has he left the faith? Before the teacher can answer, a student, Wasil ibn Ata, offers a third answer: neither. A place in between. Then he gets up, moves to another pillar, and some of the others go with him. That, at least, is the story people tell about how a group got its name: the Mu'tazilah, those who withdraw.
screen: `A HARD QUESTION IN BASRA.` → `A THIRD ANSWER.` → `THOSE WHO WITHDRAW.`

segments.voice: The Mu'tazilah were theologians who treated reason as a gift from Allah: a way to understand revelation, not a way around it. They're remembered as calling themselves the people of justice and oneness. Justice first. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant." The Mu'tazilah took that line all the way. If Allah is just, they argued, He does not punish people for what they could not help, so human beings must truly choose their own acts. Reward and punishment only make sense if the choice is really ours. Then oneness. They guarded tawhid so closely that they grew wary of anything eternal standing beside Allah. That led to the claim they're remembered for: the Qur'an is Allah's speech, and it was created, brought into being by Him. To their ears, an uncreated Qur'an sounded like a second eternal thing next to God. Their opponents heard it the other way around: the Qur'an is Allah's own speech, and His speech is not a made thing like a chair or a mountain. That disagreement didn't stay in the classroom; tomorrow it becomes a trial. But the Mu'tazili question doesn't age. If God is just, what does that say about my choices? Later theologians, Sunni and Shia, answered it in different ways, and we'll meet some of them in this part. The question, sharpened in Basra, is still on the table.
screen: `REASON AS A GIFT, NOT A RIVAL.` · `JUSTICE: ALLAH WRONGS NO ONE.` · `ONENESS: NOTHING ETERNAL BESIDE HIM.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION THAT DOESN'T AGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small unfairness from this week, something you saw or something you did, and don't solve it or judge anyone. Just ask quietly: what would a just response look like here? If you pray, you can recall the line, Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant; if you don't, the plain question is enough.
The Mu'tazilah. Those who withdraw: theologians of reason who stressed Allah's justice and oneness, and said the Qur'an was created. Today's word.
Your line: justice and reason. A just God, and choices that are really ours. See you tomorrow.

1243.title: The trial of the created Qur'an
1243.word: The trial of the created Qur'an
1243.hook: a question of theology becomes a test given by the state, and one scholar won't give the answer
1243.howItsDone: Muslims remember the mihna as the time caliphs tried to enforce the doctrine of the created Qur'an, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal is honored, especially among Sunnis, for refusing under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mu'tazilah, who stressed justice and oneness, and said the Qur'an was created.

Questions of theology usually live in books and lecture halls. You can disagree about them over dinner and still pass the bread. But for a stretch of the Abbasid caliphate, one question went to court. Judges and scholars were called in and asked, one by one: is the Qur'an created? There was a right answer, and the government had chosen it. Some said the words and went home. Some would not, and among them was a scholar in Baghdad, Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
screen: `A QUESTION GOES TO COURT.` → `IS THE QUR'AN CREATED?` → `ONE SCHOLAR WON'T SAY IT.`

segments.voice: The episode has a name in Arabic: al-mihna, the trial, or the ordeal. It began with the caliph al-Ma'mun, who took up the Mu'tazili view that the Qur'an was created and ordered officials to test the scholars on it. Those who refused could lose their posts, or worse, and the policy outlived him, carrying on under the caliphs after him. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, whose name the Hanbali school carries, kept refusing. The accounts of his life, collected by his family and students, say he was held in chains, questioned, and beaten. And they give his answer again and again, in one shape: show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. They also show what he did not do. He didn't call for a revolt, raise an army, or curse the caliph from the pulpit. He just wouldn't say the sentence. Some reports say that afterward he forgave the men who had him beaten. In time a later caliph, al-Mutawakkil, ended the policy. Two things came out of it. In Sunni theology, Ibn Hanbal's position, that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, became the standard one. And the scholars took a lesson about who settles questions of belief. A ruler had tried, with prisons and whips, and it hadn't worked. The state stepped in, and the state stepped back out. What stayed was a quiet man who kept asking for a verse.
screen: `AL-MIHNA: THE TRIAL.` · `A CALIPH CHOOSES THE ANSWER.` · `SHOW ME A VERSE.` · then, large: `THE STATE STEPPED BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little straighter, the way you might in a hard meeting, and bring to mind one thing you hold to, something you'd quietly decline to say even if it made life easier. Notice your jaw and hands, and let the shoulders drop while you keep the conviction: firmness doesn't need clenching. If you pray, ask in your own words for steadiness; if not, just keep the posture, back straight, shoulders soft.
The trial of the created Qur'an. Al-mihna: when caliphs enforced the Mu'tazili view, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused to give the answer. Today's word.
screen: `THE TRIAL OF THE CREATED QUR'AN — today's word`.

1244.title: Imam al-Ash'ari
1244.hook: a star pupil of the Mu'tazilah changes his mind, and keeps his tools
1244.howItsDone: Sunni students of theology learn about al-Ash'ari as the scholar who left the Mu'tazilah and used kalam to defend the beliefs of the people of hadith, and the Ash'ari school is named after him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the trial of the created Qur'an, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who wouldn't say the sentence.

Three brothers. One dies a faithful believer. One dies rejecting faith. The third dies as a small child. Where does each one stand on the Day of Judgment? That puzzle, the later sources say, was put by a student in Basra to his teacher, al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazili master. The student was Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who had studied Mu'tazili theology for years and could argue it with skill. By the time the conversation was over, the story goes, he had started to leave it.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS.` → `A STUDENT'S PUZZLE.` → `A MIND STARTS TO CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest as it's told. The teacher answers: the believer in a high rank, the unbeliever punished, the child somewhere safe but lower, since he did no good works. The student presses: what if the child says, Lord, why didn't You let me live long enough to earn more? The teacher says Allah knew it was better for him to die young. Then what if the brother who rejected faith cries out, why didn't You take me as a child too? The teacher has no answer. The story's point: insist that human reason can always explain what Allah's justice must do, and sooner or later you hit a question it can't answer. Historians treat this story with caution, and other reasons for his turn are told too. But the turn itself is history. Al-Ash'ari left the Mu'tazilah; some reports say he stood up in the mosque in Basra and announced it in public. What makes him matter is what he did next. He didn't throw away reason. He took the tools of kalam, the careful arguments he'd learned, and turned them toward defending what the people of hadith already held: that the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech, that His attributes are real, that believers will see Him in the life to come. Ahmad ibn Hanbal had answered with a request for a verse. Al-Ash'ari answered with the verse, and an argument to go with it. Reason in the service of tradition: that's the line he drew, and others would follow it.
screen: `A QUESTION REASON CAN'T ANSWER.` · `HE LEAVES THE MU'TAZILAH.` · `HE KEEPS THE TOOLS OF KALAM.` · then, large: `REASON FOR TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you once held firmly and see differently now, a view, a habit, a person you misjudged, and notice what changed it. Look at your old self without contempt, and, like al-Ash'ari, who kept his years of study and turned them, ask what from the old view is worth keeping. If you pray, you can thank Allah for whatever led you on.
Imam al-Ash'ari. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari: a former Mu'tazili who used reason to defend traditional belief. Today's word.
Your line: reason for tradition. He changed his mind and kept his tools. Same time tomorrow.

1245.title: The Ash'ari school
1245.hook: paper and ink, and the speech they carry: the Ash'ari middle way
1245.howItsDone: The Ash'ari school is taught in Sunni seminaries as a school of theology, and Ash'aris hold that Allah's speech is eternal while the written copies and recitations of the Qur'an are created.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Imam al-Ash'ari, who left the Mu'tazilah and put reason to work for tradition.

A printed Qur'an, open on a reading stand. Paper from a mill, ink from a factory, glue in the spine. Every bit of it was made, at a certain time, by certain hands. Someone opens it and recites, and the voice is made too: breath, throat, a person born on a certain day. So here's the question from the trial again, with the book in your hands. Is the Qur'an created? Ahmad ibn Hanbal said no, and would not say otherwise. The Mu'tazilah said yes. The school that grew from al-Ash'ari drew a line through the middle.
screen: `PAPER, INK, A VOICE.` → `ALL OF IT MADE.` → `SO IS THE QUR'AN CREATED?`

segments.voice: The Ash'ari answer goes like this. Allah's speech is one of His attributes, and like Him it's eternal, not a made thing. But the copy in your hands, the ink and paper, the sounds in your mouth when you recite, the memory of it in a child's head: all of that is created. So a printed Qur'an is something made that carries something unmade. The recitation is yours. The speech is His. That move shows the school's whole style: take a fight with two sides, and find where each side is right. With the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'aris agree that reason matters and that the things of this world are created. With the people of hadith, they agree that the Qur'an is Allah's speech and not a creature. So they're called a middle way, between reason running ahead of revelation and a refusal to reason at all. Over the centuries the school drew names that are still taught. Al-Baqillani argued for it. Al-Juwayni taught it. His student al-Ghazali, whose books are still read, wrote within it. It became tied especially with scholars of the Shafi'i and Maliki schools of law. Not everyone accepted it. Hanbali scholars, as we'll see in a couple of days, often kept their distance, and Shia theology took its own road. But the Ash'ari move is the one to keep: the ink is made, and the speech it carries is not.
screen: `HIS SPEECH IS ETERNAL.` · `THE INK AND THE VOICE ARE MADE.` · `AGREE WITH EACH SIDE WHERE IT'S RIGHT.` · then, large: `A MIDDLE WAY.`

segments.voice: If there's a Qur'an or any well-loved book nearby, rest a hand on it; if not, rest a hand on your chest. Notice the made things, the paper, the cover, your own breath and voice, and then what they carry: words and meaning that didn't start with the paper. Say quietly, the recitation is mine, the speech is His, or just hold the thought that made things can carry what isn't made.

1246.title: Imam al-Maturidi
1246.hook: a theologian in Samarqand, close to the Ash'aris, with one difference worth knowing
1246.howItsDone: The Maturidi school is studied alongside the Ash'ari school in Sunni seminaries, and it is followed especially by Hanafi scholars.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ash'ari school, a middle way, where the ink is made and the speech it carries is not.

All week the stage has been Basra and Baghdad. Now go east, past Iran, across the great river, into what is now Uzbekistan. Samarqand: a city of traders and scholars on the Silk Road. A theologian named Abu Mansur al-Maturidi taught there; his name, the sources say, comes from Maturid, a quarter of the city. He was a Hanafi, trained in the legal school of Abu Hanifa, and he wrote a book called simply Kitab al-Tawhid, the book of oneness. He worked on the same questions as al-Ash'ari, far from Basra, and reached answers that sit very close.

Start with how close the two schools are. Ash'aris and Maturidis both defend traditional Sunni belief with reason. Both say the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech, and both affirm His attributes. Later scholars often named them together as the two Sunni schools of kalam, and the Maturidi school became tied especially with Hanafi scholars. Now the one difference worth learning. Can a person know by reason alone that some things are good and some are bad, before any messenger arrives? The Ash'aris said our obligations come from revelation: without a messenger, no duty is laid on us. Al-Maturidi gave reason a bigger job. Reason, in his view, can recognize that lying is ugly and that gratitude is right, and can even grasp that the world has a Maker who deserves thanks. Revelation confirms and fills in what reason sees; it doesn't contradict it. Both schools agree that Allah is just and that the Qur'an guides. They disagree about how much the mind can see on its own. That's a fair disagreement, and Sunni scholars kept both schools in their curricula. And that rounds off a week: faith that rises and falls, kalam, the Mu'tazilah and their justice, the trial and Ahmad ibn Hanbal's refusal, al-Ash'ari's turn, his school's middle way, and now Samarqand. One conversation, carried from city to city.
